newsitem.title: UK: Rushdie condemns Denmark as cowardly for visit-ban.
newsitem.headline: Rushdie condemns Denmark as cowardly for visit-ban.

text.p: British writer Salman Rushdie, facing death threats from Iran, said on Friday the Danish government was cowardly for barring him from collecting a top European literary award in Copenhagen.
Citing security concerns, Danish authorities said they were unable to offer sufficient protection, because of advance publicity on the trip and with police stretched by a Nordic biker gang war.
Their response outraged Rushdie who said in a statement: "It is a cowardly decision which is exactly the opposite of what one should do in the face of such threats as the Iranian fatwa."

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and with permanent protection since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a death threat or fatwa against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses".
Presentation of awards to Rushdie, Austrian writer Christoph Ransmayer and Danish author and translator Thorkild Bjoernvig was to have been made on November 14 in Copenhagen.
It is this year's European Cultural Capital, a title which rotates around the EU.
"It is scandalous that Copenhagen, the present EU Capital of Culture, refuses to permit the winner of the EU's own literature prize to attend the awards ceremony," Rushdie said.
In the past two years he has travelled widely abroad and in Britain, giving lectures and attending literary events.

The writer, picked for the prize for his latest novel "The Moor's Last Sigh," said he was particularly angered by the curt note he received barring him from a country he has already visited several times.
"It was rather mysterious -- a typed text with no letter-heading. They had not even shown the courtesy of signing it," said Rushdie.
"If I'm being treated in this way, I will refuse the award. I'm not receiving it in the backroom of a pub."
Denmark's decision was also condemned in Sweden. "I have not heard of a more obvious breach of human rights in the EU," said Arne Ruth, chairman of the Swedish Rushdie Committee.
Iran says it is powerless to lift the fatwa, which can only be revoked by the man who issued it. But Khomeini died in 1989.
The European Union has made headway on blunting the fatwa since France launched a diplomatic initiative almost two years ago when it held the EU's rotating presidency.

Tehran says it would not send anyone to kill the author. But European officials say this would probably be insufficient to solve the long-running crisis without a further commitment to prevent others from doing so.
Rushdie says the dialogue has not gone far enough.

"The EU, although it has been very determined orally to get agreements, has put very few teeth into that process", he said on a visit this week to Vienna when he discussed with Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky how to step up pressure on Iran.
Rushdie, born to Moslem parents in Bombay, has always rejected Iran's charge of blasphemy against Islam.
